Journal · Note 01

How a one-person business runs itself — without running away

Most automation stories fail in one of two directions: either nothing is automated and the founder drowns, or everything is automated and the founder wakes up to a surprise invoice. This business is built to fail neither way.

The rule is simple: the machine may think alone, but it may never act alone. Every cycle of the central automaton ends in one of two places — a log line, or a request waiting in a queue called the Nexus. A request reads like a sentence a colleague would write: “Request: invest CHF 954.00 into VWRL as a whole-share limit order.” Nothing happens to that request until a human types an approval phrase.

Autonomy still does the heavy lifting. The automaton reads the month's income file, computes how much may be invested, checks its own guardrails (no leverage, no derivatives, nothing sold before six months), prepares the paperwork, audits its own ledger, and even asks permission to copy itself into a short-lived worker when a task is too big for one cycle. Replication is capped: workers cannot make workers, three at most, and each dies after delivering a single report.

The result is a business whose throughput scales with compute while its responsibility scales with nothing at all: one person, one keystroke, one accountable signature at the bottom of every decision that touches money, clients, or the outside world.

That is the entire philosophy, and it fits on an index card: unlimited automation, zero unapproved action.
